headline: Curaleaf keeps win as Sixth Circuit refuses to rehear $31.8M case
dek: The court on 17 November declined to revisit its ruling that federal courts cannot enforce cannabis supply contracts, leaving a $31.8 million verdict voided.
key_points: The Sixth Circuit denied Hello Farms' request for rehearing on 17 November, The Marijuana Herald reported, citing Law360, leaving its September ruling for two Curaleaf subsidiaries in place.

In that published 10 September opinion, the court threw out a $31.8 million jury award, holding that federal courts cannot enforce agreements to commit federal drug crimes, even where state law allows the business.

The panel said the April 2026 move of state medical marijuana to Schedule III does not rescue a contract made in 2020, and would not by itself legalise a sale between businesses without DEA registration.
The ruling binds federal courts in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky and Tennessee; Hello Farms' remaining option is to ask the US Supreme Court to hear the case.
body: A Michigan grower that won a $31.8 million jury verdict against two Curaleaf subsidiaries will not get it back from the Sixth Circuit. The US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit on 17 November denied Hello Farms Licensing MI's request to reconsider a September decision that erased the award, according to The Marijuana Herald, which cited a Law360 report. The denial leaves the court's published opinion as binding law across Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky and Tennessee.

That opinion, filed on 10 September in Hello Farms Licensing MI v. GR Vending MI (No. 25-1759), holds that federal courts cannot enforce a contract whose performance would be a federal drug crime, even when both sides are licensed under state law. For cannabis operators, it means a federal judge may refuse to make a buyer pay for product it agreed to take, and that a breach in a falling market can go unpunished in federal court.

According to the opinion, GR Vending MI and CURA MI, both Curaleaf Holdings subsidiaries, signed an output contract in November 2020 to buy everything Hello Farms grew in its 2020 and 2021 harvests. CURA MI acted as guarantor. The parties expected 12,000 to 15,000 pounds from the 2020 crop, and GR Vending paid a refundable $2.2 million deposit. At the time Hello Farms held only a Michigan medical grower's licence, while GR Vending held both medical and adult-use retail licences.

The 2020 harvest came in at about 16,300 pounds, and all of it passed the contract's testing terms, the court said. GR Vending took the first shipment of roughly 2,000 pounds. By January 2021 wholesale prices were collapsing, and GR Vending stopped accepting deliveries. Hello Farms sold the rest to a third party at lower prices, then expanded from 7 to 25 acres, obtained recreational licences and sold a 2021 crop of about 37,500 pounds to the same buyer, again for less than the contract would have paid.

Hello Farms sued in February 2021. The case was moved to federal court in Bay City, where Judge Matthew Leitman rejected the defendants' argument that the deal was illegal under federal law, calling it a close call. A jury found for Hello Farms and awarded $31.8 million. With prejudgment interest the judgment reached about $37.2 million, according to The Marijuana Herald.
> The Sixth Circuit has made federal court the one venue where a cannabis buyer can walk away from a signed deal.
## Why the court threw it out

Circuit Judge Nalbandian wrote the opinion, joined by Judge Siler; Judge Hermandorfer joined all but one part. The court said the effect of federal illegality on a contract is a question of federal law even in a case between private parties under state law, and that courts have a duty not to lend their power to illegal bargains. The panel acknowledged that the illegality defence is unattractive, calling it in the Supreme Court's old phrase a dishonest one, but said public policy, not fairness to the defendant, drives it.

The court rejected the district judge's view that the deal was a protected medical marijuana contract. It held that the Rohrabacher-Farr rider, which Congress has renewed every year since 2014, only stops the Justice Department from spending money to block state medical programmes. In the panel's reading the rider does not legalise anything, does not grant immunity, and would leave past conduct open to prosecution if Congress ever restored the funding. It listed other federal consequences the rider leaves untouched, including Section 280E, bankruptcy access and trademarks.

Hello Farms also pointed to the Justice Department's April 2026 final rule moving FDA-approved marijuana products and state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III. The panel gave two reasons that rule changes nothing here. First, a contract's legality is judged when it is made, and the rule is not retroactive; this deal predates it by more than five years. Second, the rule itself requires DEA registration to grow or distribute medical marijuana lawfully, so the same contract signed today between unregistered businesses would still break federal law, the court said.

The court also set aside the Supreme Court's 2026 remarks in United States v. Hemani about falling federal enforcement. Lower enforcement and wider public acceptance, the panel said, do not change what the statute says. It noted that the federal sentencing commission recorded 386 marijuana trafficking sentences in 2025.

The practical reach is wide. The opinion lists district courts that have refused to enforce investment agreements, business purchases, seed deals and equity promises tied to marijuana. Supply contracts, earn-outs, landlord disputes and M&A indemnities between plant-touching companies in the four Sixth Circuit states now face the same risk if a dispute lands in federal court, where diversity jurisdiction often sends cross-state cases.

The ruling also sharpens the value of DEA registration. As we reported on 6 November, the DEA has registered about 900 medical dispensaries in seven states. By the panel's own reasoning, registration is what separates a lawful medical transaction from an illegal one under federal law, which may make registered counterparties more attractive for contracts written today. That is our inference; the court did not decide whether a contract between registered businesses would be enforceable.

For Curaleaf, the result removes a liability of about $37 million that had been sitting on two Michigan subsidiaries. For growers who sell into a falling wholesale market, it removes a remedy. Contracts that pick state courts and arbitration, rather than federal court, may become more common, though the opinion does not address how state judges should treat the same defence.

Hello Farms can ask the US Supreme Court to take the case. Under the Court's rules a petition is normally due 90 days after a rehearing denial, which points to mid-February 2027. Watch whether other circuits follow the Sixth Circuit, and whether any registered medical operators test the question the panel left open. Watch Congress too: the opinion says it is up to lawmakers, not courts, to give retroactive effect to contracts made under state law.
